title: From Nobody To History: The Story Of Engelbert Dollfuss
description:

Engelbert Dollfuss (alternatively Dollfuß; 4 October 1892 – 25 July 1934) was an Austrian politician and dictator who served as chancellor of Austria between 1932 and 1934. Having served as Minister for Forests and Agriculture, he ascended to Federal Chancellor in 1932 in the midst of a crisis for the conservative and nationalist government.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of Engelbert Dollfuss — in that order. As a result of his consistent opposition to Nazi demands, Dollfuss was assassinated on 25 July 1934 by a group of Austrian Nazis, including Otto Planetta, Franz Holzweber, Rudolf Prochaska, and Paul Hudl, who entered the Chancellery building and shot him in an attempted coup d'état. Having served as Minister for Forests and Agriculture, he ascended to Federal Chancellor in 1932 in the midst of a crisis for the conservative and nationalist government.

Setbacks came early for Engelbert Dollfuss, and the response to them is the real story. This crisis culminated in the self-elimination of the Austrian Parliament, a coup sparked by the resignation of the presiding officers of the National Council. Suppressing the Socialist movement in the Austrian Civil War and later banning the Austrian Nazi Party, he cemented his rule through the First of May Constitution in 1934.

The legacy of Engelbert Dollfuss outlived the circumstances that produced it. Later that year, Dollfuss was assassinated as part of a failed coup attempt by Nazi agents. Dollfuss was born to a poor, lower middle-class peasant family in the hamlet of Great Maierhof in the commune of St.

Few lives travel as far as that of Engelbert Dollfuss, and the distance is the point. Young Dollfuss spent his childhood in his step-father's house in the nearby commune of Kirnberg, where he also went to elementary school. The local parish priests helped to finance Dollfuss's education, as his parents were unable to do so by themselves alone.

The childhood of Engelbert Dollfuss contains the adult in small print. After graduating from high school, Dollfuss intended to become a priest, and thus he enrolled at the University of Vienna to study theology, but after a few months changed course and started studying law in 1912. He became a member of the Students' Social Movement, a student organisation dedicated to social and charitable work among the workers.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of Engelbert Dollfuss — in that order. As World War I broke out, Dollfuss was reported to be recruited in Vienna but was rejected because he was two centimetres shorter than the minimum. Fully grown, he was less than 1.52 m (5 ft 0 in) in height, and later was nicknamed "Millimetternich", a portmanteau of Millimeter (German for millimeter) and Klemens von Metternich.

The turning point in the life of Engelbert Dollfuss looked like a failure at the time. The same day he was rejected in Vienna, Dollfuss went to St. Pölten where the recruiting commission for his district was located and insisted on being recruited, and, even though he did not meet the minimum height standards, he was accepted.

Every biography of Engelbert Dollfuss has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. As a volunteer, he had a right to choose a regiment in which he would serve, and Dollfuss opted for the Tyrolese militia also known as the Kaiserschützen. In September 1914 he graduated from the Brixener Officer's School with the rank of Ensign and was transferred to the Imperial-Royal 2nd Tyrolian Rifle (Landesschützen) Regiment in Bosen.

The education of Engelbert Dollfuss happened mostly outside any school. Over the course of the war, he was awarded the Silver Bravery Medal 1st Class (1916), the Karl Troop Cross (1917), the Wound Medal with one wound stripe and the Bronze Military Merit Medal twice, the Military Merit Cross 3. Class with War Decoration and Swords (1918) and, after the war, the Austrian War Memorial Medal with Swords.

What Engelbert Dollfuss wanted at the start and what Engelbert Dollfuss got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. After the war, he was still a student and was employed by the Lower Austrian Peasants' Union, which helped him to secure his material existence, and it was here where Dollfuss gained his first political experience. Being recognised for the abilities he showed at the Union, he was sent for further studies to Berlin.

The defining trait of Engelbert Dollfuss was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. In Berlin, he began to garner dislike for some of his professors, as academia there was substantially influenced by liberalism and socialism. In his studies, he devoted himself to the Christian principles of economics.

Those who met Engelbert Dollfuss at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. In Germany, he became a member of the Federation of German Peasants' Union and of the Preussenkasse – essentially, a central bank for member cooperatives, where he gained practical experience. In Germany, he met his future wife Alwine Glienke, a descendant of a Pomeranian family.

The private years of Engelbert Dollfuss explain the public decades better than any speech. Dollfuss often met with Carl Sonnenschein, leader of social activities of students and the pioneer of the Catholic movement in Berlin. After returning to Vienna, he was a secretary of the Lower Austrian Peasants' Union.

The family Engelbert Dollfuss came from matters more than the legends admit. A few years later, he was a representative of Austria at the International Agrarian Congress, where his proposals made him internationally known in that sphere. On 1 October 1930 Dollfuss was appointed the president of the Federal Railways, the largest industrial corporation in Austria.

The first real success of Engelbert Dollfuss arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. In March 1931, he was appointed Federal Minister of Agriculture and Forestry. On 10 May 1932, Dollfuss, aged 39 and with only one year's experience in the Federal Government, was offered the office of Chancellor by President Wilhelm Miklas, also a member of the Christian-Social Party.

The last chapter of Engelbert Dollfuss was written long after the fame. Dollfuss did not immediately respond, instead spending the night in his favourite church praying, returning in the morning for a bath and a spartan meal before finally replying to the President that he would accept the offer. Dollfuss was sworn in on 20 May 1932 as head of a coalition government between the Christian-Social Party, the Landbund – a right-wing agrarian party – and Heimatblock, the parliamentary wing of the Heimwehr, a paramilitary ultra-nationalist group.

The whole life of Engelbert Dollfuss reads like a single decision repeated. The coalition assumed the pressing task of tackling the problems of the Great Depression. Much of the Austro-Hungarian Empire's industry had been situated in the areas that became part of Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia after World War I as a result of the Treaty of Saint-Germain.

Between the birth and the legend of Engelbert Dollfuss lie the years that actually decide it. In March 1933, a constitutional impasse arose over irregularities in the voting procedure in the Austrian parliament. The  Social Democratic president of the  National Council (the lower house of parliament), Karl Renner, resigned to be able to cast a vote as a parliament member.

The reputation of Engelbert Dollfuss was built in the middle, not at the edges. As a consequence, the two vice presidents, belonging to other parties, resigned as well in order to be able to vote. Dollfuss took the three resignations as a pretext to declare that the National Council had become unworkable and advised  President Wilhelm Miklas to issue a decree adjourning it indefinitely.

Somebody like Engelbert Dollfuss should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. On March 7, Dollfuss announced his government had assumed emergency powers based on the "Wartime Economy Authority Law," which had been passed in 1917. From that point onwards, he governed by emergency decree, effectively seizing dictatorial powers.

To understand where Engelbert Dollfuss ended up, start with where Engelbert Dollfuss began. Dollfuss banned the Communist Party of Austria on 26 May 1933 and the DNSAP on 19 June 1933. Under the banner of the  Fatherland Front, he later established a one-party dictatorship rule largely modelled after fascism in Italy, banning all other Austrian parties – including the  Social Democratic Labour Party (SDAPÖ).

The road from the beginning to the peak of Engelbert Dollfuss ran through years nobody filmed. Social Democrats however continued to exist as an independent organization, nevertheless, though without its paramilitary Republikanischer Schutzbund, which until banned on 31 March 1933 could have mustered tens of thousands against Dollfuss's government. Dollfuss modelled the Fatherland Front according to Catholic corporatist ideals with  anti-secularist tones and in a similar way to Italian fascism, dropping Austrian pretenses of unification with Germany as long as the Nazi Party remained in power there.

Each stage of the life of Engelbert Dollfuss made the next stage possible. According to Frank McDonough, the Fatherland Front "resembled a Fascist party with its similar uniforms, a copycat swastika symbol and salutes, but it had no antisemitic policies". In August 1933, Benito Mussolini's regime issued a guarantee of Austrian independence.

The people who knew Engelbert Dollfuss young describe someone already restless. Dollfuss also exchanged "Secret Letters" with Mussolini about ways to guarantee Austrian independence. Mussolini had an interest in Austria forming a buffer zone against Nazi Germany.

Meanwhile, Dollfuss was opposed both to the Nazi Party and to any left-wing force, and would soon go on to wage a "two-front war" against the Nazis and Social Democrats at home. Dollfuss was shot and wounded in an assassination attempt on 3 October 1933 by Rudolf Dertil, a 22-year-old who had been ejected from the military for his pro-Nazi views and had joined the Nazi Party in 1932.

By the time Engelbert Dollfuss reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. In the aftermath of the attempted assassination, Dollfuss declared martial law, which allowed for the resumption of capital punishment in Austria. In its drive to eliminate the Social Democrats' Schutzbund, the Dollfuss government searched the homes and meeting places of its members for weapons.

On 12 February 1934, the Austrian Civil War was sparked by the armed resistance of the Linz branch of the Social Democrats to the search of their party headquarters. Word of the fighting in Linz spread quickly, and additional armed conflicts broke out, primarily in Austria's industrial regions and Vienna.

Setbacks came early for Engelbert Dollfuss, and the response to them is the real story. The Schutzbund was greatly outnumbered by the police and army, which used artillery against the insurgents. In addition, the general strike which had been called to support the uprising failed to materialize.

The result was the collapse of the rebellion by 15 February, with the deaths of about 350 persons, roughly equally divided between civilians, insurgents, and government forces. The Social Democrats were outlawed by the Federal government on 12 February 1934, and their leaders were imprisoned or fled abroad.

Dollfuss staged a rump parliamentary session with just Fatherland Front members present in April 1934 to  have a new constitution approved, effectively the second constitution in the world espousing corporatist ideas (after that of the Portuguese Estado Novo). The session retrospectively made all the decrees already passed since March 1933 legal.
